sublevels.description: Heat engine where the combustion of a fuel occurs with an oxidizer in a combustion chamber that is an integral part of the working fluid flow circuit. In particular Diesel and Otto Engines. Turbomachines are a separate concept.

sublevels.name: Turbomachines
sublevels.description: Describes machines that transfer energy between a rotor and a fluid, including both turbines and compressors. While a turbine transfers energy from a fluid to a rotor, a compressor transfers energy from a rotor to a fluid

sublevels.name: Marine Engineering
sublevels.description: Marine engineering includes the engineering of boats, ships, and any other marine vessel or structure, as well as oceanographic engineering. Not to be confused with Offshore Engineering (Civil Engineering).

sublevels.name: Process Engineering
sublevels.description: Process engineering focuses on the design, operation, control, optimization and intensification of chemical, physical, and biological processes

sublevels.name: Engineering Thermodynamics, Heat and Mass Transfer
Research Methods in Language and Linguistics
Languages
sublevels.description: Language is a means of communicating complex ideas or feelings. Although human language can be verbal or non-verbal, it is more complex than any form of animal communication and reflects the culture of its speakers.

sublevels.name: Classical Linguistics
sublevels.description: covers old Greek/Latin/other languages (Yoka)

sublevels.name: Literary Diction
sublevels.description: Diction is a writer's or speaker's distinctive vocabulary choices and style of expression in a literary work, poem or story. In its common meaning, it is the distinctiveness of speech.

sublevels.name: Anthropology
sublevels.description: Anthropology is the study of humans, their close relatives and their cultural environment. Subfields of anthropology deal with hominin evolution and the comparative study of extant and past cultures.

sublevels.name: Restoration Ecology
sublevels.description: Restoration ecology is the scientific study supporting the practice of ecological restoration, which is the practice of renewing and restoring degraded, damaged, or destroyed ecosystems and habitats in the environment by active human intervention and action.

sublevels.name: Forestry
sublevels.description: Forestry is the study and practice of the cultivation and management of woodlands. Forests provide goods and services such as timber, recreation and carbon sequestration.

sublevels.name: Wood Science and Technology
sublevels.description: The study of the science and technology of wood and other lignocellulosic materials.

sublevels.name: Forest Ecology
sublevels.description: Forest ecology is the study of all aspects of the ecology of wooded areas, including rainforest, deciduous and evergreen, temperate and boreal forest. It includes the community ecology of the trees and other plant and non-plant species, as well as ecosystem processes and conservation.

sublevels.name: Forestry Management
sublevels.description: Forestry management is the process of planning and implementing practices for the stewardship and use of forests and other wooded land to meet specific environmental, economic, social and cultural objectives. It deals with the overall administrative, economic, legal, social, technical and scientific aspects related to natural and planted forests.

sublevels.name: Tree Biology
sublevels.description: The study of tree structure and function, and the relationship between them.

sublevels.name: Conservation Biology
sublevels.description: Conservation biology or Conservation Ecology is a mission-oriented science that focuses on how to protect and restore biodiversity, or the diversity of life on Earth. Like medical research, conservation biology deals with issues where quick action is critical and the consequences of failure are great. To preserve biodiversity, scientists must answer three general questions. First, how is the diversity of life distributed around the planet? Second, what threats does this diversity face? Third, what can people do to reduce or eliminate these threats and, when possible, restore biological diversity and ecosystem health?

sublevels.name: Ecosystems
sublevels.description: Ecosystem ecology is the combined study of the physical and biological components of ecosystems. It focuses on how matter and energy flow through both organisms and the abiotic components of the environment.

sublevels.name: Marine Biology
sublevels.description: Marine biology is the study of life in the oceans and brackish waters, which ranges from archaea and bacteria to marine mammals, and includes organisms such as corals that affect the shape of the seafloor. This may also include human modifications to ocean biology, such as fisheries or the effects of overfishing.

sublevels.name: Marine Mammals
sublevels.description: Marine mammals are those whose life cycle is at least in part dependent on the ocean. They include cetaceans, such as whales and dolphins, sirenians, such as dugongs and manatees, pinnipeds, such as seals and walruses, and also partially marine species such as polar bears and sea otters.

sublevels.name: Fisheries
sublevels.description: Fisheries are social, biological and geographical objects involved in producing fish for human consumption. They are usually united by a common geographical area, catch technique and/or target species, and fisheries science is the study of factors affecting catch and stock sustainability.

sublevels.name: Coral Reefs
sublevels.description: Coral reefs are marine structures created by calcifying coral animals and their algal symbionts. Coral reef ecosystems are generally high in biodiversity, most often found in shallow tropical seas, and are threatened by factors including ocean acidification, global warming and sea level rise.

sublevels.name: Ecosystem Services
sublevels.description: Ecosystem services are the benefits and functions that natural ecosystems provide to people. They include provision of food and clean water, pollination of crops, climate regulation and ecotourism.

sublevels.name: Theoretical and Statistical Ecology
sublevels.description: Theoretical ecology is the scientific discipline devoted to the study of ecological systems using theoretical methods such as simple conceptual models, mathematical models, computational simulations, and advanced data analysis. Statistical ecology deals with the development of new methodologies for analyzing ecological data.

sublevels.name: Landscape Ecology
sublevels.description: Landscape ecology is the study of the pattern and interaction between ecosystems within a region of interest, and the way the interactions affect ecological processes, especially the unique effects of spatial heterogeneity on these interactions.

sublevels.name: Molecular Ecology
sublevels.description: Molecular ecology is the use of molecular genetic tools to study ecological questions. Techniques such as microarrays and DNA markers are used to study the interactions and diversity of natural populations.

sublevels.name: Terrestial Ecology
sublevels.description: Terrestrial ecology is the study of how land-based organisms interact with each other and their environment.

sublevels.name: Tropical Ecology
sublevels.description: Tropical ecology is the study of all aspects of the ecology of tropical areas, which are those found approximately 23.5 degrees either side of the Equator. Notable tropical ecosystems include the rainforests of Amazonia, Africa and South East Asia, savannah grasslands and coral reefs.

sublevels.name: Macroecology
sublevels.description: Macroecology is the study of broad scale ecological patterns and processes. The focus is rarely on single communities and ecosystems, and instead looks at principles that apply more broadly such as metabolic scaling, extinction risk and diversity gradients.

sublevels.name: Agroecology
sublevels.description: Agroecology is the study of the ecology of terrestrial agricultural systems. It includes both the effects of agricultural practices such as pesticide use on non-domesticated species, and the effect of the ecological environment on crop and livestock yields.

sublevels.name: Community and Population Ecology
sublevels.description: Community ecology is the study of communities formed of populations of different species. It includes the study of the interactions between species, such as mutualism, predation and competition, and the dynamics and structure of the community.

sublevels.name: Ecological Network
sublevels.description: Ecological networks are representations of the interactions that occur between species within a community. The interactions include competition, mutualism and predation, and network properties of particular interest include stability and structure.

sublevels.name: Food Web
sublevels.description: Food webs are ecological networks of consumption interactions, including the relationships between different trophic levels such as primary producers, herbivores, predators and decomposers. Key areas of the study of food webs are their stability and how energy and nutrients flow through them.

sublevels.name: Freshwater and Marine Ecology
sublevels.description: Biolimnology or freshwater ecology is the study of all aspects of the ecology of terrestrial aquatic systems, including rivers, lakes and ponds. It includes the community ecology of these ecosystems, as well as ecosystem processes, interactions with adjacent terrestrial and marine ecosystems, and conservation and restoration..Freshwater ecology is the study of all aspects of the ecology of terrestrial aquatic systems, including rivers, lakes and ponds. It includes the community ecology of these ecosystems, as well as ecosystem processes, interactions with adjacent terrestrial and marine ecosystems, and conservation and restoration.

sublevels.name: Plant Ecology
sublevels.description: Science of the functional relationships between plants and their habitats

sublevels.name: Climate-Change Impacts
sublevels.description: Climate-change impacts are the consequences of climate change – both expected and realised – for natural and human systems. Climate impacts research is typically interdisciplinary and frequently involves the construction of climate impact models. Some key research themes include: ecology, water resources, agriculture, human heath, the economy and built infrastructure.

sublevels.name: Paleoecology
sublevels.description: Palaeoecology is the study of past ecosystems using palaeontological methods. Fossil data are used to reconstruct interactions between different species and between species and their environment.

sublevels.name: Boreal Ecology
sublevels.description: Boreal ecology is the study of ecosystems in the subarctic (boreal) zone of the Northern hemisphere. These areas are dominated by coniferous forest, generally have permafrost soils, and occur below the Arctic tundra latitudes.

sublevels.name: Sustainability
sublevels.description: Sustainability is essentially the ability to endure, for example by exploiting resources in a way that does not deplete their future availability or unduly damage the wider environment. This concept has been incorporated in the idea of sustainable development.

sublevels.name: Microbial Ecology
sublevels.description: Microbial ecology is the study of the interactions of microorganisms with their environment, each other, and plant and animal species. It includes the study of symbioses, biogeochemical cycles and the interaction of microbes with anthropogenic effects such as pollution and climate change.

sublevels.name: Biodiversity
sublevels.description: Biodiversity is the variation in living forms and can be measured in ways that include the number of species, functional variety of species, evenness of species distribution or genetic diversity. Biodiversity science investigates levels of biodiversity, its functional effects, and how and why it changes over time.

sublevels.name: Environmental Social Sciences
sublevels.description: Environmental social science is the application of social science – broadly the study of the relationship between individuals in their context within society – and its application to our understanding of environmental issues.

sublevels.name: Climate Change Ecology
sublevels.description: Climate-change ecology is the study of the effects of anthropogenic climate change on any aspect of ecology. It includes the effects of altered temperature and precipitation on the distribution, abundance, behaviour and physiology of populations and communities.

sublevels.name: Energy and Society
sublevels.description: Studies the interaction of issues related to energy (including supply and demand, ethics, economic effects, etc.) with the society in a holistic way.

sublevels.name: Energy Justice
sublevels.description: Energy justice applies justice principles to energy policy and security, its production and systems, energy consumption through the society, and energy activism, and is strongly related to sustainable living and mitigation of climate change.

sublevels.name: Environmental Policy
sublevels.description: Studies the commitment of an organization or government to the laws, regulations, and other policy mechanisms concerning environmental issues.

sublevels.name: Climate-Change Adaptation
sublevels.description: Climate-change adaptation encompasses a broad range of human policies and activities primarily intended to reduce the risks posed by climate change. It includes both realised and expected risks.

sublevels.name: Environmental Impact
sublevels.description: Defined as any change to the environment, caused by development, industry or infrastructure, or by the release of certain substances in the environment.

sublevels.name: Climate-Change Policy
sublevels.description: Climate-change policy encompasses policies formulated specifically to tackle climate change and can be local, national or international in scope. These broadly fall into two categories; those designed to minimise the extent of climate change – climate change mitigation – and those intended to minimise risks and seize upon new opportunities – climate change adaptation.

sublevels.name: Socioeconomic Scenarios
sublevels.description: Socioeconomic scenarios are plausible representations of the future based on coherent, and internally consistent, assumptions about the evolution of key social and economic drivers. Examples of these drivers are economic growth, technological development and population. They are not intended to be predictive, but are designed to explore the implications of different futures.

sublevels.name: Environmental Economics
sublevels.description: Environmental economics is the study of the economics of ecological and environmental issues. It focuses on the monetary value of ecosystems and the costs and benefits of environmental policies.

sublevels.name: Climate-Change Impacts
sublevels.description: Climate-change impacts are the consequences of climate change – both expected and realised – for natural and human systems. Climate impacts research is typically interdisciplinary and frequently involves the construction of climate impact models. Some key research themes include: ecology, water resources, agriculture, human heath, the economy and built infrastructure.

sublevels.name: Climate Change Mitigation
sublevels.description: Climate-change mitigation encompasses policies and activities intended to reduce the greenhouse gas forcing of the climate system. Key intervention points include: the reduction of greenhouse gas sources, for example by reducing deforestation; emissions, for instance low carbon energy generation; and enhancing greenhouse gas sinks, for example by changes in land use.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Family, Youth and Aging
Research on Racism, Anti-Semitism and Extremism
Urban Geography and Urbanism
sublevels.description: incl. megacities, cities, towns

sublevels.name: HIV infections
sublevels.description: HIV infections (human immunodeficiency virus infections) include the spectrum of infections caused by the virus HIV that range from asymptomatic seropositivity to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)-related complex (ARC) and AIDS.

sublevels.name: Health Policy
sublevels.description: Health policy is the set of decisions and plans, developed by governmental or nongovernmental agencies, designed to promote specific health-care objectives. Policies can be directed at individuals, physicians, pharmaceutical companies, or health-care systems. Examples include tobacco control policies and those designed to promote equal opportunites to access care.

sublevels.name: Health Economics
sublevels.description: Health economics is a branch of economics concerned with issues related to efficiency, effectiveness, value and behavior in the production and consumption of health and healthcare.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Religion
sublevels.description: The Sociology of Religion is the study of religious practices, beliefs, and communities using the methods, tools, and analytical frameworks employed in the discipline of sociology.

sublevels.name: Quality of Life Research
sublevels.description: Quality of life is the standard of health, life satisfaction, life chances, and happiness experienced by individuals or groups. It implies the lack or the availability of various social and economic opportunities, rights and entitlements, equity, security that affect the life, health and happiness of people. The concept includes physical, emotional, social and psychological parameters.

sublevels.name: Fitness and Exercise Culture
sublevels.description: Fitness and Exercise Culture refers to the cultural and social factors and effects of fitness and physical exercise and is concerned with the ways in which people attribute meaning to sports activities through shared and culturally prescribed interpretative patterns.  It covers sports as a mass phenomenon and generally recognised and commerzialised types of sport, as well as communities of less popular and/or special and distinctive types of sport. This includes Lifestyle-, Health- and aesthetic aspects.

sublevels.name: Outdoor Activity
sublevels.description: Outdoor activity refers to any leasure time activity characterised by being conducted outdoors, mostly in natural settings. They may be performed for physical or mental exercise, as well as for collective or personal enjoyment or enjoyment of the natural environment. Thus, the aspects of athleticism and competition are usually less emphasized. Examples are Bicycling, Fishing, Hiking, Hunting, canoeing etc.

sublevels.name: Adventure Sports
sublevels.description: Types of sport performed mostly outdoors, in exceptional or hazardous environments, involving high degree of physical risk and bodily exertion due to height or speed. Characterised less by competition among athletes, than by great physical challenges, unusual experiences and/or highly spezialized athletic skills. Examples are Rock climbing, Mountainbiking, Canyoning, Surfing, Skydiving, Motocross etc.

sublevels.name: Physical Recreation
sublevels.description: Physical recreation refers to a way of conducting sports or any kind of physical exercise for reasons of physical and mental regeneration and health, leasure, improvement of body awareness, social and team interaction, enhancement of self-discipline, perseverance and self-motivation as well as for personal experience of a sense of achievement. Most types of sport may be performed as physical recreation, however in a less organised, competitive and physically demanding way.

sublevels.name: Geoinformatics
sublevels.description: Geoinformatics or Digital Geography is the science and technology dealing with the structure and character of spatial information, its capture, its classification and qualification, its storage, processing, portrayal and dissemination, including the infrastructure necessary to secure optimal use of this information.

sublevels.name: Gerontology
sublevels.description: Gerontolotgy comprises the sociological aspects of elderly individuals' lives. Furthermore it addresses cultural, psychological, cognitive, and biological aspects of ageing and an aging population.

sublevels.name: Social Justice
sublevels.description: Social justice is a concept of fair and just relations between the individual and society, as measured by the distribution of wealth, opportunities for personal activity, and social privileges.

sublevels.name: Well-Being
sublevels.description: Well-being is the experience of health, happiness and prosperity, a sense of purpose in life, high life satisfaction, and the ability to manage stress.

sublevels.name: Sport Sociology
sublevels.description: Sport Sociology is a discipline of sociology which in research and theory deals with Sport as a social phenomenon, the interrelations between individual actions and societal structures in sport, and the place of sports on society and the ever changing societal conditions. Like many other specialized subdisciplines of Sociology, Sport Sociology approaches its object of study strictly empirically and is oriented towards the formation of theory. Topics studied in Sport Sociology include communication and interaction on Sport and sport groups, social roles, expectations and attitudes towards sport, the process of socialisation in with and through sport, systems of values and norms, mass media representations and the social history of sport.

sublevels.name: Sport Career
sublevels.description: Sport Career primarily  refers to the career of an athlete, but might also refer to the occupational career of a person working in a wider context of sport. A career or professional career is the personal career of a person in his or her professional life. While the term career is generally understood to designate a change in qualification and income and is therefore related to social and economic upwards mobility, Sport Careers are similarly linked to the accumulation of accompolishments in sports and accompanying opportunities.

sublevels.name: Sports Economics
sublevels.description: Sports Economics is the study of issues of sports by means of economics, its methods and theoretical frameworks (heavily based on macroeconomics) as well as the study of economics problems in the context of sports. Sports Economics attempts to describe, explain and prognosticate actions by relevant parties and use the acquired knowledge technologically.

sublevels.name: Fitness and Exercise Culture
sublevels.description: Fitness and Exercise Culture refers to the cultural and social factors and effects of fitness and physical exercise and is concerned with the ways in which people attribute meaning to sports activities through shared and culturally prescribed interpretative patterns.  It covers sports as a mass phenomenon and generally recognised and commerzialised types of sport, as well as communities of less popular and/or special and distinctive types of sport. This includes Lifestyle-, Health- and aesthetic aspects.

They may be performed for physical or mental exercise, as well as for collective or personal enjoyment or enjoyment of the natural environment. Thus, the aspects of athleticism and competition are usually less emphasized. Examples are Bicycling, Fishing, Hiking, Hunting, canoeing etc.

Characterised less by competition among athletes, than by great physical challenges, unusual experiences and/or highly spezialized athletic skills. Examples are Rock climbing, Mountainbiking, Canyoning, Surfing, Skydiving, Motocross etc.

sublevels.name: Physical Recreation
sublevels.description: Physical recreation refers to a way of conducting sports or any kind of physical exercise for reasons of physical and mental regeneration and health, leasure, improvement of body awareness, social and team interaction, enhancement of self-discipline, perseverance and self-motivation as well as for personal experience of a sense of achievement. Most types of sport may be performed as physical recreation, however in a less organised, competitive and physically demanding way.

sublevels.name: Sport History
sublevels.description: Sport History aims at analyzing the sporting past by following socially relevant questions with the help of methodic instruments of historical science. It is concerned with historical events related to sports, the development of contemporary sport and its various cultural origins and predecessors, as well as with the shifting meaning of sport for individuals and social groups across time.

sublevels.name: Sport Psychology
sublevels.description: Sport Psychologyis is concerned with the preconditions and determining factors of the behaviour and experience of individuals (persons) in sport.  It aims at the adequate unterstanding of the behaviour and the experience of individuals in sport by describing and measuring consistency and variability, by offering explanations, as well as by determining their preconditions and possibilities to predict and shape its future course.  More specifically, Sport Psychology explores the processes of perception and decision making during sports games, the emergence or reduction of emotions (such as fear), the determining factors of an active lifestyle, the impact of sport on the development of children or the personality and group features of successful athletes and teams.

sublevels.name: Mental Training
sublevels.description: The term Mental Training is used to describe a variety of psychological methods, which aim at facilitating and improving performance, resilience, self-awareness, confidence or well-being by optimising social and communicative skills, cognitive skills or motivational and emotional processes.   In Sport Psychology, the narrow definition of Mental Training specifies it as training procedures for optimising the regulation of movement by conciously and repeatedly envisioning movement tasks or actions. Mental Training may also include techniques to regulate emotion (anger, fear, stress), motivation (will, achievement motivation) or perception (focus, concentration) and strengthen the athletes confidence in his or her capability. This may also include techniques that focus on coach-athlete or team interaction. Besides the long term systematic application of mental training, it is also used situationally in competition preparation or evaluation.

sublevels.name: Sport Theory
sublevels.description: Sport Theory encompasses theoretical knowledge and analysis in the fields of biology, training theory, kinematics, as well as psychological, social and sociopolitical aspects of sport. In this regard, Sport theory draws on concepts from political sciences and sociological theories (such as theories of conflict and exchange, funcionalist, interactionalist, critical and feminist or figurational theories),  as well on concepts from philosophy end ethics to understand and explain the significance of sport in a more fundamental way.

sublevels.name: Sports Ethics
sublevels.description: Sports Ethics deals with any type of ethical issue, questions or problem in the context of Sport and attempts to suggest sensible courses of actions in order to alleviate or regulate these problems and establish ethical standards. Ethical issues in Sports commonly concern performance enhancing drugs (doping), Gender Discrimination, Fair Play, Responsibility for the performance, Fan Behaviour, Diversity or Protection of athletes health and safety.

sublevels.name: Sport Training
sublevels.description: Sport Training refers to the special process of preparation of athletes and sports persons based on scientific principles aimed at improving and maintaining higher performance capacity in different sports activities. Training is designed to improve overall fitness and the abilities necessary to perform in a given sport, which might include strength training, practice of movement patterns, corrective and restorative exercises, conditioning and cardiovascular training, mental and psychological training and advise on nutrition. Sport training is usually an individual-specific process aided by scientific methods and findings and supported by a coaching person. It therefore involves some degree of education of the athlete and not only aims at improvement of physical fitness, but also at the acquisition of specific sports skills, improvement of tactical efficiency and mental abilities.

sublevels.name: Individual Sport
sublevels.description: Individual Sport is any sport which is practiced either by a single person (e.g. running) or by two opposing individuals (e.g. tennis). Competition in individual sports is also characterised by competing individuals rather than competing in teams. This allows athletes to aim for personal goals and has various effects on training strategies, tactics and the overall significance and prominence of individual athletes in individual sports.

sublevels.name: Team Sport
sublevels.description: Team sport includes any sport where individuals are organized into opposing teams of two or more members interacting directly and simultaneously in competition to win. The team members act together toward a shared objective and usually fulfill different roles and take positions with specific tasks and functions during a game. Examples of team sports are soccer, basketball, baseball, rugby or hockey.

sublevels.name: Sports Biomechanics
sublevels.description: Sports Biomachanics refers to the description, detailed analysis and assessment of human movement during sport activities. Sport Biomachanics applies the laws of machanics to sport movements in order to explain how and why the human body moves in the way that it does and how the athletes body interacts with sports equipment and the environment during movement. Sport Biomachanics helps to gain unterstanding of athlete performance, as well as to minimise risk of injury, and increase performance. It usually includes detailed quantitative analysis of athletes movements by means of measurement, mathematical modelunf or computer simulation.

sublevels.name: Sports Neuromuscular Physiology
sublevels.description: Sports Neuromuscular Physiology is concerned with the physiology of the (human) Neuromuscular System, which links the central nervous system to the peripheral nervous system and is composed of a neural circuit including motor neurons in the spinal cord, sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglion, and skeletal muscle fibers. With regard to the context of sport, neuromuscular physiology is concerned with the relation between neuromuscular coupling, stimulation and muscle contraction during sport or exercise.

sublevels.name: Motor Control
sublevels.description: Motor control refers to the process by which the nervous system coordinates the muscle and limbs to achieve a desired movement or set of actions. This includes the ability to anticipate, adjust and respond to deviations from the desired action.

sublevels.name: Cerebellum
sublevels.description: The cerebellum is part of the hindbrain that is located below the temporal and occipital lobes of the cerebral cortex. It consists of a thin, densely folded cerebellar cortex surrounding the deep cerebellar nuclei. It has important roles in motor control and motor learning, and also non-motor functions in language, cognitive processing and emotion.

sublevels.name: Basal ganglia
sublevels.description: The basal ganglia are a set of subcortical structures that interact with the cerebral cortex to regulate motor, cognitive and affective function through reinforcement learning and action selection. Its input structure, the striatum, receives a dense dopaminergic input that is critical for reinforcement learning and whose dysfunction contributes to motor and cognitive pathologies.

sublevels.name: Neuromuscular junction
sublevels.description: The neuromuscular junction is a specialized synapse between motor neurons and the muscle fibre they innervate. In vertebrates, the postsynaptic side is referred to as the endplate and contains a high-density of cholinergic receptors that facilitate synaptic transmission.

sublevels.name: Premotor Cortex
sublevels.description: The premotor cortex is an area of the motor cortex just anterior to the primary cortex. Although like the primary motor cortex, it sends direct projections to the spinal cord, the premotor cortex is primarily involved in the planning of actions.

sublevels.name: Central Pattern Generators
sublevels.description: A central pattern generator (CPG) is a neuronal network in which interconnected excitatory and inhibitory neurons produce an oscillating, rhythmic output in the absence of sensory feedback. CPGs play an important part in motor behaviour such as breathing, swimming and locomotion.

sublevels.name: Spine Plasticity
sublevels.description: Spine plasticity is the biological process by which neuronal activity leads to short- or long-term changes in the morphology, appearance or disappearance of dendritic spines – the specialized protrusions on a neuron’s dendrites that are the sites of excitatory synaptic input. Spine plasticity has been implicated in mediating synaptic plasticity.

sublevels.name: Motor Cortex
sublevels.description: The motor cortex is the region of the cerebral cortex including the primary motor, premotor and supplementary motor cortices that is responsible for planning and executing actions.

sublevels.name: Spine Motility
sublevels.description: Spine motility is the biological process by which a neuron’s dendritic spines – the specialized protrusions that are the sites of excitatory synaptic input – alter their morphology, appear or disappear. Spine motility is regulated by numerous factors and is thought to require remodelling of the actin cytoskeleton.

sublevels.name: Brain-machine Interface
sublevels.description: A brain–machine interface (BMI) is a device that translates neuronal information into commands capable of controlling external software or hardware such as a computer or robotic arm. BMIs are often used as assisted living devices for individuals with motor or sensory impairments.

sublevels.name: Spine Structure
sublevels.description: Spine structure is the shape and composition of a dendritic spine. Dendritic spines are small protrusions from the dendritic shaft. Although their structure is variable, a typical spine consists of a spine head that may be mushroom- or cup-shaped and a thinner neck region. Each spine contains elements of the postsynaptic apparatus.

sublevels.name: Sport Kinematics
sublevels.description: Sport Kinematics is the study of the spatial and temporal expression of motion in sport. Kinematics is the study of the geometric and time-dependent aspects of motion. It describes different forms of motion, distinguishable with regard to the geometrical aspect (e.g. translation motion, rotation motion) and types of motion (e.g. uniform, non-uniform), regarding the temporal aspect. Kinematics therefore uses physical parameters such as velocity and acceleration, without analyzing causes (forces) and effects of motion.

sublevels.name: Sports Medicine
sublevels.description: Sports Medicine is a subfield of medicine dealing with physical fitness and the treatment and prevention of injuries in sports and exercise. Although its origins lie in the clinical treatment of athletes, Sports Medicine traditionally also encompasses matters of performance physiology and methods of training control.

sublevels.name: Sport Orthopaedics
sublevels.description: Sport Orthopaedics is a medical subspecialty of Orthopedics and Sports medicine. It focuses on the investigation, preservation, restoration and health care in general pertaining structures of the musculoskeletal system affected by athletic activity. Activities of Sport Othopedics include diagnosis of your injury or disorder, Treatment with medication, exercise, surgery or other treatment plans, rehabilitation through exercises or physical therapy to restore movement, strength and function, as well as prevention of injury or deceleration of progressing diseases.

sublevels.name: Physiotherapy
sublevels.description: Physiotherapy is a health profession as well as a treatment method that focuses on the science of movement and helps people to restore, maintain and maximize their physical strength, function, motion and overall well-being by addressing the underlying physical issues. Physiotherapy aims at preventing injury and disability, managing acute and chronic conditions, Improving and maintaining optimal physical performance, Rehabilitating injury and the effects of disease or disability and Educating patients to prevent re-occurrence of an injury. For these purposes, Physiotherapy applies a variety of techniques, such as manual manipulation, electrical nerve stimulation, acupuncture, functional testing or provision of assistive, adaptive, supportive and protective devices and equipment.

sublevels.name: Sports Pharmacology
sublevels.description: Sports pharmacology includes study of the various aspects of the drug use and abuse (Doping) in sports and treatment of sports-related injuries. There are a variety of medications which are commonly used in a sports medicine setting. These are usually used to manage pain or in an attempt to reduce inflammation. Commonly abused agents in sports include anabolic–androgenic steroids and its analogs, blood, erythropoietin, growth hormone and its derivatives, nutritional supplements, creatine, amphetamines, beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate (HMB), stimulants, and analgesics.

sublevels.name: Disability Sport
sublevels.description: Disability Sport refers to the aim to guarantee full participation of disabled persons (including physical and intellectual disabilities) into sport life, as practising sport not only covers the therapeutic and medical intentions generally defined as treatment, but also the social and educational aspects. Accordingly, disability sports or parasports, are sports played by persons with a disability (physical, mental, permanent and temporary). As many disabled sports are based on existing able bodied sports, modified to meet the needs of persons with a disability, they are sometimes referred to as adapted/adaptive sports.

sublevels.name: Fitness
sublevels.description: Fitness is generally understood as physical and also mental well-being. Altough being a vague concept without any measurable determinants, there are different factors contributing to overall fitness. In medicine, fitness refers to the physical, mental and emotional general condition of a person in relation to the performance demands placed on them from outside. From this perspective, fitness is affected by physical performance potential, intelligence, emotional stability, state of the immune system, reproducibility and Adaptability in case of lack of resources.

sublevels.name: Sport Physiology
sublevels.description: Sport physiology is the study of how exercise alters the function and structure of the body (physical and biomechanical), by applying concepts from the medical fields of Anatomy (the study of basic bodily structure and the interrelationships between various body parts) and Physiology (the study of the processes or functions of living things, or the study of body functions) to a context of sports and exercise. It is primarily the study of how the body adapts physiologically to the acute or short term stress of exercise, and the chronic or long term stress of physical training, but also specifically focuses at the athletes training and enhancing athlete performance within a specific sport.

sublevels.name: Sport Analytics
sublevels.description: Sport Analytics refers to the use of data and statistical methods to measure and evaluate performance for the purpose of being able to make decisions to improve performance and gain advantage over competing teams or athletes. Sport analytics is used during and prior to sport events and can inform players, coaches and other parties in aspects of game tactics, player fitness and health as well as the business of a sports organisation.

sublevels.name: Sports Communication
sublevels.description: Sports communication is an area of study that seeks to understand the relationship between communication processes and sport contexts. Communication processes refer to the creation and understanding of meaning through exchanging verbal and nonverbal messages. It can encompass the study of interpersonal and organizational communication between players, coaches, managers, referees, trainers and physiotherapists, and governing bodies, as well as communication between sports participants, fans, and the media and way in which sports are represented and communicated in the media. the methods used to study Sports Communication range from quantitative over qualitative approaches up to frameworks in critical and cultural studies. Studies in sports communication have addressed subjects such as audience reactions to mediated sporting contests; communication between coaches and athletes; media portrayals of athletes based on considerations such as gender, race, and nationality; and the professional routines of sports media practitioners.

sublevels.name: Sports Nutrition
sublevels.description: Sports Nutrition is an interdisciplinary field of study concerned with the understanding of the body's use of nutrients during athletic competition (and the need for nutritional supplements), as well as the practical use of proper nutrition and dietary supplements to enhance athletic performance. Works in the field of Sports Nutrition commonly apply knowledge nutrition science, dietology, biochemistry, exercise physiology, cell and molecular biology. For instance, studies in Sports Nutrition focus on the different types and quantities of fluids and food taken by an athlete, and also deals with the consumption of nutrients such as vitamins, minerals, supplements and organic substances that include carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

sublevels.name: Sport Sociology
sublevels.description: Sport Sociology is a discipline of sociology which in research and theory deals with Sport as a social phenomenon, the interrelations between individual actions and societal structures in sport, and the place of sports on society and the ever changing societal conditions. Like many other specialized subdisciplines of Sociology, Sport Sociology approaches its object of study strictly empirically and is oriented towards the formation of theory. Topics studied in Sport Sociology include communication and interaction on Sport and sport groups, social roles, expectations and attitudes towards sport, the process of socialisation in with and through sport, systems of values and norms, mass media representations and the social history of sport.

sublevels.name: Sport Career
sublevels.description: Sport Career primarily  refers to the career of an athlete, but might also refer to the occupational career of a person working in a wider context of sport. A career or professional career is the personal career of a person in his or her professional life. While the term career is generally understood to designate a change in qualification and income and is therefore related to social and economic upwards mobility, Sport Careers are similarly linked to the accumulation of accompolishments in sports and accompanying opportunities.

sublevels.name: Sport Technology
sublevels.description: Sport Technology is a area of study connecting sport science and engineering. Some subfields of Sport Technology are equipment and clothic technology, sports informatics, Sports measurement technology or Performance Diagnostics. Sport Technology might refer to any of the different uses of technical resources and devices in a sport context. Technology is applied to assist athletes, rehabilitate after injuries and increase performance, either during sport activities in the form of specialized gear or in preparation, evaluation and training (e.g. self monitoring, data bases, data evaluation). Technology is also applied for monitoring, broadcasting and to assist referees (usually in the form of computer software and cameras), as well as to manipulate the sporting environment (arena architecture, sport tracks/fields etc.)  Technology affects many aspects of sport from performance on and off the field to spectating and public profile. The use of technology in Sport is therefore ambivalent and might have positive and negative impact on sport from the perspective of athletes, officials or spectators

sublevels.name: Rehabilitation Psychology
sublevels.description: Rehabilitation is the process of restoring normal function and improving quality of life for individuals following a disease or an injury. Rehabilitation is commonly used to treat people after a sports injury, spinal cord injury, stroke, or orthopaedic surgery.

sublevels.name: Trafficking
sublevels.description: DEPRECATED

sublevels.name: Theory and Method in Social Work
Chemistry Publishing
sublevels.description: Chemistry publishing and communication is the creation and dissemination of information that covers the discipline of chemistry. This topic covers, for example, editorial and publication processes (such as peer review), discussion of how information should be presented, methods of sharing data and the evolution of publishing as a business.

sublevels.name: History of Chemistry
sublevels.description: The history of chemistry is rich, evolving from early discussions on the nature of matter in ancient Egypt and Greece, through to the emergence of alchemy, the development of the periodic table and quantum chemistry.

sublevels.name: Radiology
sublevels.description: Radiology, Medical Imaging or Diagnostic Radiology: comprises different imaging modalities and processes to image human body for diagnostic and treatment purposes. It is also used to follow the course of a disease already diagnosed and/or treated.

sublevels.name: Panoramic Radiography
sublevels.description: A panoramic radiograph is a panoramic scanning dental X-ray of the upper and lower jaw.

sublevels.name: Endoscopy
sublevels.description: Endoscopy is an optical imaging technique that uses a rigid or flexible small diameter light guide inserted into an organ, cavity or tissue for light delivery and collection.

sublevels.name: Colonoscopy
sublevels.description: Colonoscopy is the examination of the lining of the large intestine, or colon, using a thin, flexible tube with a camera and light on its end called a colonoscope. Abnormal tissue may be biopsied or removed during the procedure.

sublevels.name: Microendoscopy
sublevels.description: Microendoscopy is a type of endoscopy that uses optical fibres or fibre bundles in conjunction with microscopy techniques to obtain microscopic images of tissue immediately adjacent to the imaging end of the endoscope inserted into the body.

sublevels.name: Oesophagogastroscopy
sublevels.description: Oesophagogastroscopy is the examination of the lining of the esophagus and stomach using a thin, flexible tube with a camera and light on its end called an endoscope. It allows diagnosis and therapeutic intervention for conditions of the upper digestive tract.

sublevels.name: Video capsule endoscopy
sublevels.description: Video capsule endoscopy is a type of endoscopy that uses a magnetically guided wireless capsule to image inside hollow organs or body cavities.

sublevels.name: Magnetic Resonance Imaging
sublevels.description: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive biomedical imaging technique that uses a strong oscillating magnetic field to induce endogenous atoms such as hydrogen, or exogenously added contrast agents, to emit radiowaves that are detected and used to generate two and three-dimensional images of a living subject in the MRI scanner.

sublevels.name: Whole Body Imaging
sublevels.description: Whole-body imaging is typically performed using MRI or PET. It involves a single procedure to produce an internal image of the body for diagnostic purposes.

sublevels.name: Diffusion Tensor Imaging
sublevels.description: Diffusion tensor imaging is a magnetic resonance imaging method that measures the diffusion patterns of molecules in biological tissue. These patterns provide information on the microscopic structure of the tissue. The technique is commonly used to image neuronal fibre tracts.

sublevels.name: Functional magnetic resonance imaging
sublevels.description: Functional magnetic resonance imaging is a non-invasive method for measuring brain activity. It uses magnetic resonance imaging to map blood oxygenation levels in the brain and estimate changes in blood flow that are correlated with brain activity.

sublevels.name: Radionuclide Imaging
sublevels.description: Radionuclide imaging is the production of images of internal body parts obtained by cameras that detect the radioactive emissions of an injected radionuclide as it has distributed differentially throughout body tissues. Images obtained with a moving detector are called scans, whereas images obtained with a stationary camera device are called scintiphotographs.

sublevels.name: Molecular Imaging
sublevels.description: Molecular imaging encompasses a variety of imaging techniques that rely on the use of exogenously added probes to target and detect desired cellular or molecular processes in a living organism.

sublevels.name: Radiography
sublevels.description: Radiography is the use of X-rays or gamma rays to examine non-uniformly composed material; images are recorded on a sensitized surface, such as photographic film or a digital detector. Medical radiography includes examination of any part of the body for diagnostic purposes, such as detecting fractures or a bowel obstruction.

sublevels.name: Tomography
sublevels.description: Tomography is a technique whereby the body is imaged in 'slices' or sections. Typically the imaging modality is X-ray radiography, and the slices can be viewed separately or in combination.

sublevels.name: Positron-Emission Tomography
sublevels.description: Positron-emission tomography (PET) is a technique for imaging the metabolic activity of internal tissues in three dimensions based on biologically active tracer compounds conjugated to positron-emitting radionuclides that are typically injected in the blood. It can be used to study cancer metastasis, brain and heart function.

sublevels.name: Computed Tomography
sublevels.description: Computed tomography is a method of examining body organs by scanning them with X rays and using a computer to construct a series of cross-sectional scans along a single axis.

sublevels.name: Three-Dimensional Imaging
sublevels.description: Three-dimensional imaging is a technique that combines many scans (from computed tomography, MRI or ultrasonography) computationally. Such images can then be manipulated by the radiographer or physician to aid diagnosis and surgical planning.

sublevels.name: Neuroradiology
sublevels.description: Neuroradiology, Neuroimaging or Brain Imaging. Brain imaging refers to the usually non-invasive or minimally invasive techniques that enable imaging the structure or function of the brain. Brain imaging techniques take advantage of X-rays, radioactive labelling, magnetic fields induced by the brain?s electric activity, or optical absorption or paramagnetic properties of haemoglobin.

sublevels.name: Magnetoencephalography
sublevels.description: Magnetoencephalography (MEG) is a non-invasive biomedical functional brain imaging technique that uses sensitive magnetometers to measure the tiny magnetic fields generated by natural electrical signals in the brain. This is used to produce maps of spontaneous or evoked brain activity.

sublevels.name: Functional magnetic resonance imaging
sublevels.description: Functional magnetic resonance imaging is a non-invasive method for measuring brain activity. It uses magnetic resonance imaging to map blood oxygenation levels in the brain and estimate changes in blood flow that are correlated with brain activity.

sublevels.name: Bone Scintigraphy
sublevels.description: Bone Scintigraphy, Bone Imaging or Bone Scan is a study that uses various quantitative and qualitative methods to visually assess the composition, structure and metabolism of skeletal bone.

sublevels.name: Cardiography
sublevels.description: Cardiography or Cardiac Imaging

sublevels.name: Radiation Oncology
sublevels.description: Radiotherapy, or radiation therapy, is the clinical use of high energy rays (ionizing radiation) to induce DNA damage in all exposed cells to ultimately kill cancer cells or prevent cancer growth. Radiotherapy may be used to eradicate some cancers, to reduce recurrence or as palliative treatment.

sublevels.name: Biological Imaging
sublevels.description: Imaging is the visual representation of a subject. Imaging methods may provide a two-dimensional depiction of a surface or a three-dimensional reconstruction, they may use special probes or modalities to track specific molecular features, and they may use invasive or non-invasive means to visualize the internal components of a subject.

sublevels.name: Time-lapse Imaging
sublevels.description: Time-lapse imaging is a technique whereby serial images are taken at regular time points to capture the dynamics of what is being observed. Recorded images can be played back at different speeds to aid analysis.

sublevels.name: X-ray Tomography
sublevels.description: X-ray tomography, or X-ray computed tomography, is a method for generating 3-dimensional imaged volumes from 2-dimensional X-ray image slices. X-ray imaging is based on the differential absorption or scattering of an X-ray source to reveal the internal attributes of a structure or specimen; it is commonly used in medical imaging.

sublevels.name: Viral Tracing
sublevels.description: Viral tracing is a method that uses viral movement between cells as a label to determine the cells? connectivity. Viruses are most commonly used as tracers to define neural circuitry.

sublevels.name: Fluorescence Imaging
sublevels.description: Fluorescence imaging is the visualization of fluorescent dyes or proteins as labels for molecular processes or structures. It enables a wide range of experimental observations including the location and dynamics of gene expression, protein expression and molecular interactions in cells and tissues.

sublevels.name: Wide-Field Fluorescence Microscopy
sublevels.description: Wide-field fluorescence microscopy is a fluorescence imaging technique that relies on illumination of the entire field of view of a fluorescence microscope and simultaneous detection of the emitted fluorescence using a camera.

sublevels.name: Fluorescent Probes
sublevels.description: Fluorescent probes are molecules that absorb light of a specific wavelength and emit light of a different, typically longer, wavelength (a process known as fluorescence), and are used to study biological samples. The molecules, also known as fluorophores, can be attached to a target molecule and act as a marker for analysis with fluorescence microscopy.

sublevels.name: Cellular Imaging
sublevels.description: Cellular imaging encompasses the techniques that allow the detection and analysis of cellular organelles and macromolecules. Cellular imaging observations are obtained using light-based or electron-based microscopes and often request further analysis with computer based programming.

sublevels.name: Optical Biological Imaging
sublevels.description: Optical imaging includes a variety of imaging techniques that rely on illumination light in the ultraviolet, visible and infrared regions of the electromagnetic spectrum. The term typically excludes classical microscopy techniques in favour of larger scale imaging methods that rely on the detection of ballistic or diffusive photons, or the photoacoustic effect.

sublevels.name: Bioluminescence Imaging
sublevels.description: Bioluminescence imaging (BLI) is a technology that uses light emitted by enzyme-catalyzed reactions to report activity at the molecular level. Bioluminescent reporters require a small chemical substrate for non-invasive imaging in cell biology and small animal studies. BLI does not require incident light like fluorescence or phosphorescence, avoiding phototoxicity.

sublevels.name: 3-D Image Reconstruction
sublevels.description: 3D reconstruction is the process of generating a computer model of the 3D (3-dimensional) appearance of an object from a set of two-dimensional images. It is common in computer vision. In medicine, for example, it uses serial sections generated by computed tomography (CT), electron microscopy or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

sublevels.name: Computational Neuroscience
sublevels.description: Computational neuroscience includes both the study of the information processing functions of the nervous system, and the use of digital computers to study the nervous system. It is an interdisciplinary science that links the diverse fields of neuroscience, cognitive science and psychology, electrical engineering, computer science, physics and mathematics. (Ken).Computational neuroscience is the field of study in which mathematical tools and theories are used to investigate brain function. It can also incorporate diverse approaches from electrical engineering, computer science and physics in order to understand how the nervous system processes information.

sublevels.name: Neural decoding
sublevels.description: Neural decoding is the study of what information is available in the electrical activity (action potentials) of individual cells or networks of neurons. Studies of neural decoding aim to identify what stimulus, event, or desired output elicits a particular pattern of neural activity.

sublevels.name: Dynamical Systems
sublevels.description: Dynamical systems describe an ensemble of particles whose state varies over time and thus obeys differential equations involving time derivatives. In order to make a prediction about the system’s future behavior, an analytical solution of such equations or their integration over time through computer simulation is realized..In mathematics dynamical systems refer to dynamical systems theory, an area of mathematics used to describe the behavior of the complex dynamical systems, usually by employing differential equations or difference equations. This theory deals with the long-term qualitative behavior of dynamical systems, and studies the nature of, and when possible the solutions of, the equations of motion of systems that are often primarily mechanical or otherwise physical in nature, such as planetary orbits and the behaviour of electronic circuits, as well as systems that arise in biology, economics, and elsewhere. Much of modern research is focused on the study of chaotic systems

sublevels.name: Complex Networks
sublevels.description: Complex networks are networks that feature patterns of connection between their elements that are neither purely regular nor purely random. Most real-world networks, such as transportation, social or gene-regulatory networks, are complex.

sublevels.name: Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos Theory
sublevels.description: Nonlinear Dynamics and its applications aims to solve different problems coming from many fields as chemistry, medicine, biology and engineering. It is the branch of physics that studies systems governed by equations more complex than the linear, aX+b form. Nonlinear systems, such as the weather or neurons, often appear chaotic, unpredictable or counterintuitive, and yet their behaviour is not random.Chaos theory focuses on the behavior of dynamical systems that are highly sensitive to initial conditions. It is an interdisciplinary theory stating that within the apparent randomness of chaotic complex systems, there are underlying patterns, constant feedback loops, repetition, self-similarity, fractals, self-organization, and reliance on programming at the initial point known as sensitive dependence on initial conditions.

sublevels.name: Ergodic Theory
sublevels.description: Ergodic theory is a branch of mathematics that studies dynamical systems with an invariant measure and related problems. A central concern of ergodic theory is the behavior of a dynamical system when it is allowed to run for a long time.

sublevels.name: Time Series Analysis
sublevels.description: A time series is a sequence of measurements performed at successive points in time. Time series can be used to derive models to predict future values based on previously observed values. Time series are used in statistics, signal processing, pattern recognition, econometrics, mathematical finance, weather forecasting, earthquake prediction, electroencephalography, control engineering, astronomy, communications engineering, and largely in any domain of applied science and engineering which involves temporal measurements

sublevels.name: Network Models
sublevels.description: Network models are a computer architecture, implementable in either hardware or software, meant to simulate biological populations of interconnected neurons. These models, also known as perceptrons or multilayer connectionist models, process information based on the pattern and strength of the connections among the neuron-like units that compose them.

sublevels.name: Learning algorithms
sublevels.description: A learning algorithm is a mathematical framework or procedure that calculates the best output given a particular set of data. It does this by updating the calculation based on the difference between the actual and desired output. These algorithms are typically concerned with representation and generalization of the input data.

sublevels.name: Biophysical Models
sublevels.description: A biophysical model is a simulation of a biological system using mathematical formalizations of the physical properties of that system. Such models can be used to predict the influence of biological and physical factors on complex systems.

sublevels.name: Neural encoding
sublevels.description: Neural encoding is the study of how neurons represent information with electrical activity (action potentials) at the level of individual cells or in networks of neurons. Studies of neural encoding aim to characterize the relationship between sensory stimuli or behavioural output and neural signals.

sublevels.name: Tomography
sublevels.description: Tomography is a technique whereby the body is imaged in 'slices' or sections. Typically the imaging modality is X-ray radiography, and the slices can be viewed separately or in combination.

sublevels.name: Positron-Emission Tomography
sublevels.description: Positron-emission tomography (PET) is a technique for imaging the metabolic activity of internal tissues in three dimensions based on biologically active tracer compounds conjugated to positron-emitting radionuclides that are typically injected in the blood. It can be used to study cancer metastasis, brain and heart function.

sublevels.name: Whole Body Imaging
sublevels.description: Whole-body imaging is typically performed using MRI or PET. It involves a single procedure to produce an internal image of the body for diagnostic purposes.

sublevels.name: Computed Tomography
sublevels.description: Computed tomography is a method of examining body organs by scanning them with X rays and using a computer to construct a series of cross-sectional scans along a single axis.

sublevels.name: Neuroradiology
sublevels.description: Neuroradiology, Neuroimaging or Brain Imaging. Brain imaging refers to the usually non-invasive or minimally invasive techniques that enable imaging the structure or function of the brain. Brain imaging techniques take advantage of X-rays, radioactive labelling, magnetic fields induced by the brain?s electric activity, or optical absorption or paramagnetic properties of haemoglobin.

sublevels.name: Magnetoencephalography
sublevels.description: Magnetoencephalography (MEG) is a non-invasive biomedical functional brain imaging technique that uses sensitive magnetometers to measure the tiny magnetic fields generated by natural electrical signals in the brain. This is used to produce maps of spontaneous or evoked brain activity.

sublevels.name: Functional magnetic resonance imaging
sublevels.description: Functional magnetic resonance imaging is a non-invasive method for measuring brain activity. It uses magnetic resonance imaging to map blood oxygenation levels in the brain and estimate changes in blood flow that are correlated with brain activity.

sublevels.name: Computed Tomography
sublevels.description: Computed tomography is a method of examining body organs by scanning them with X rays and using a computer to construct a series of cross-sectional scans along a single axis.

sublevels.name: Climate Change
sublevels.description: Climate change refers to a statistically defined change in the average and/or variability of the climate system, this includes the atmosphere, the water cycle, the land surface, ice and the living components of Earth. The definition does not usually require the causes of change to be attributed, for example to human activity, but there are exceptions.

sublevels.name: Climate Change Management
sublevels.description: Holistic and integrated way of managing climate change, including mitigation, adaptation, and risk management.

sublevels.name: Climate-Change Policy
sublevels.description: Climate-change policy encompasses policies formulated specifically to tackle climate change and can be local, national or international in scope. These broadly fall into two categories; those designed to minimise the extent of climate change – climate change mitigation – and those intended to minimise risks and seize upon new opportunities – climate change adaptation.

sublevels.name: Climate and Earth System Modelling
sublevels.description: Climate and Earth system modelling is the use of mathematical representations of key components and properties of the atmosphere, ocean and biosphere to construct computer models. These models – which can range significantly in their complexity, depending on their intended application – are used to simulate important aspects of the Earth system and indicate how they may change in the future.

sublevels.name: Climate-Change Impacts
sublevels.description: Climate-change impacts are the consequences of climate change – both expected and realised – for natural and human systems. Climate impacts research is typically interdisciplinary and frequently involves the construction of climate impact models. Some key research themes include: ecology, water resources, agriculture, human heath, the economy and built infrastructure.

sublevels.name: Climate Change Mitigation
sublevels.description: Climate-change mitigation encompasses policies and activities intended to reduce the greenhouse gas forcing of the climate system. Key intervention points include: the reduction of greenhouse gas sources, for example by reducing deforestation; emissions, for instance low carbon energy generation; and enhancing greenhouse gas sinks, for example by changes in land use.

sublevels.name: Ultrasonography
sublevels.description: Ultrasound is a non-invasive imaging technique that uses the differential reflectance of acoustic waves at ultrasonic frequencies to detect objects and measure distances. It is commonly used for medical imaging of internal organs and developing fetuses during pregnancy. + Ultrasonography is an imaging technique that uses the reflections of high-frequency sound waves to create an image of a structure located within the body.

sublevels.name: Echocardiography
sublevels.description: Echocardiography is ultrasonography of the heart. The procedure is usually performed by placing an ultrasound-emitting transducer against the chest (transthoracic echocardiography), but can also be undertaken using an ultrasound-emitting transducer on the end of a scope that is placed in the lower part of the oesophagus (transoesophageal echocardiography).

sublevels.name: Atmospheric Science
sublevels.description: Atmospheric science is the study of the dynamics and chemistry of the layers of gas that surround the Earth, other planets and moons. This encompasses the interactions between various parts of the atmosphere as well as interactions with the oceans and freshwater systems, the biosphere and human activities.

sublevels.name: Atmospheric Dynamics
sublevels.description: Atmospheric dynamics encompasses all physical processes within atmospheres, including global and regional-scale circulation, convection, tropical and extratropical cyclones, and interannual variability. Information about atmospheric dynamics informs both short range weather forecasting and projections for medium to long term climate change.

sublevels.name: Meteorology
sublevels.description: Meteorology is the scientific study of the atmosphere that focuses on weather processes and forecasting.

sublevels.name: Atmospheric Optics
sublevels.description: Atmospheric optics is a branch of optics and photonics that studies how light behaves in the Earth’s atmosphere. This can include both understanding naturally occurring effects involving sunlight and the propagation and distortion of electromagnetic signals through air.

sublevels.name: Atmospheric Chemistry
sublevels.description: Atmospheric chemistry is the study of the components of planetary atmospheres, particularly that of the Earth. It specifically looks at the composition of planetary atmospheres and the reactions and interactions that drive these dynamic and diverse systems. The topic encompasses lab-based studies, field measurements and also their modelling.

sublevels.name: Climate and Earth System Modelling
sublevels.description: Climate and Earth system modelling is the use of mathematical representations of key components and properties of the atmosphere, ocean and biosphere to construct computer models. These models – which can range significantly in their complexity, depending on their intended application – are used to simulate important aspects of the Earth system and indicate how they may change in the future.

sublevels.name: Signal Processing
sublevels.description: Signal processing is the transmission of information with a modification, so that the new form of information may be exploited by downstream devices, as in sound converted to nerve impulses from ear to neurons. The scientific study of signal processing implicates information theory and is key to telecommunications or biology.

sublevels.name: Image Processing
sublevels.description: Image processing is manipulation of an image that has been digitised and uploaded into a computer. Software programs modify the image to make it more useful, and can for example be used to enable image recognition.

sublevels.name: Image Processing
sublevels.description: Image processing is manipulation of an image that has been digitised and uploaded into a computer. Software programs modify the image to make it more useful, and can for example be used to enable image recognition.

sublevels.name: Population Dynamics
sublevels.description: Population dynamics is the branch of life sciences that studies the size and age composition of populations as dynamical systems, and the biological and environmental processes driving them. It is the study of how and why populations change in size and structure over time. Important factors in population dynamics include rates of reproduction, death and migration. Population dynamics has traditionally been the dominant branch of mathematical biology

sublevels.name: Pattern Recognition Receptors in Plants
sublevels.description: Pattern recognition receptors are a family of cell surface receptors that bind conserved molecular structures present in pathogens. They play important roles in defence by mediating cellular responses to pathogens.

sublevels.name: Patterning
sublevels.description: A pattern is a regularity in the world, man-made design, or abstract ideas. As such, the elements of a pattern repeat in a predictable manner. A geometric pattern is a kind of pattern formed of geometric shapes and typically repeated like a wallpaper design. Geometric patterning is the study of such patterns (mathematics Springer).Patterning describes the processes by which the plan for later development of a plant is laid down. It involves the early establishment of 'prepatterns' of 'morphogens' which form a complex signalling network, which in turn determines further differentiation (Nature)

sublevels.name: Data Mining
sublevels.description: Data mining is a field of study within machine learning, and focuses on exploratory data analysis through unsupervised learning. Data mining is the process of extracting potentially useful information from data sets. It uses a suite of methods to organise, examine and combine large data sets, including machine learning, visualisation methods and statistical analyses. Data mining is used in computational biology and bioinformatics to detect trends or patterns without knowledge of the meaning of the data.

sublevels.name: Computer Ethics
sublevels.description: Value considerations in the realms of Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, Cryptology and Data Security.

sublevels.name: Sound Studies
sublevels.description: Sound studies is an interdisciplinary field that focuses largely on the emergence of the concept of "sound" in Western modernity, with an emphasis on the development of sound reproduction technologies.

sublevels.name: Human Migration
sublevels.description: Human migration is the movement of people from one place to another intending to settle in a new geographic region.

sublevels.name: Public-Private Partnership
sublevels.description: Public–private partnerships are collaborations between publicly funded organizations and for-profit organizations.

sublevels.name: Environmental Policy
sublevels.description: Studies the commitment of an organization or government to the laws, regulations, and other policy mechanisms concerning environmental issues.

sublevels.name: Diplomatics
sublevels.description: Diplomatics is a scholarly discipline centred on the critical analysis of documents – particularly, but not exclusively, historical documents.

sublevels.name: History of Germany and Central Europe
History of World War II and the Holocaust
Russian, Soviet, and East European History
World History, Global and Transnational History
Digital Marketing
sublevels.description: Digital Marketing and Marketing on Social Media

sublevels.name: Diversity Management and Women in Business
Household Finance
