sublevels.name: Market Intelligence
sublevels.description: Market analysis seeks to understand the dynamics of markets, with the goal of informing business strategies.

sublevels.name: Big Data
sublevels.description: Big data is a term used to refer to data sets that are too large or complex for traditional data-processing application software to adequately deal with. Data with many cases (rows) offer greater statistical power, while data with higher complexity (more attributes or columns) may lead to a higher false discovery rate

sublevels.name: Business IT Infrastructure
sublevels.description: set of IT components, physical compontents, software, network components

sublevels.name: Business Process Management
sublevels.description: Initiating, planning, executing, and controlling IT and business processes.

sublevels.name: Corporate Finance
sublevels.description: Corporate finance is an area of finance that deals with sources of funding, the capital structure of corporations, the actions that managers take to increase the value of the firm to the shareholders, and the tools and analysis used to allocate financial resources. The primary goal of corporate finance is to maximize or increase shareholder value.

sublevels.name: Risk Management
sublevels.description: Financial Risk Management or Risk management is the identification, evaluation, and prioritization of risks (defined in ISO 31000 as the effect of uncertainty on objectives) followed by coordinated and economical application of resources to minimize, monitor, and control the probability or impact of unfortunate events or to maximize the realization of opportunities

sublevels.name: Mergers and Acquisitions
sublevels.description: Mergers and acquisitions (M&A) involve the buying, selling, dividing and combining of different companies to achieve company goals.

sublevels.name: Accounting
sublevels.description: Accounting includes procedures for the systematic recording and evaluation of all quantifiable relationships and processes of the company for the purpose of planning, managing and controlling operational activities.

sublevels.name: Business Taxation and Tax Law
sublevels.description: "Business Taxation/Tax Law" refers to the company level, i.e. all tax issues that directly affect companies. Tax law is a sub-area of financial law. Target groups: specialist lawyers, tax consultants, and all persons concerned with tax issues in companies.

sublevels.name: Auditing
sublevels.description: Auditing means the auditing of the financial reporting of companies in accordance with the applicable accounting standards, within the framework of the audit of annual financial statements required by law.   Target groups: professionals in accounting and finance departments, corporate management and reporting

sublevels.name: Licensing
sublevels.description: Licensing is widely used in the commercialization of intellectual property such as patents on drugs or technologies. The owner of the intellectual property grants the licensee the rights to use the intellectual property, typically in return for a payment, such as a fee or royalty.

sublevels.name: Behavioral Sciences and Psychology
sublevels.description: Psychology is a scientific discipline that focuses on understanding mental functions and the behaviour of individuals and groups.

sublevels.name: Social Psychology
sublevels.description: Social psychology or Psychosocial Studies is the attempt to understand and explain how the thoughts, feelings, and behaviours of individuals are influenced by the actual, imagined, or implied presence of other human beings. (Allport, 1954)

sublevels.name: Decision Making
sublevels.description: Decision making is the process of choosing among alternatives associated with different outcomes. Deciding among multiple options can take the form of selecting a course of action or judging among ideas.

sublevels.name: Habituation
sublevels.description: Habituation occurs upon repeated presentation of stimulus such that the innate physiological or behavioural response to that stimulus is gradually diminished.

sublevels.name: Bipolar Disorder
sublevels.description: Bipolar disorder is a mood disorder that includes at least one manic episode, characterized by elevated or agitated mood and often reduced need for sleep accompanied by episodes of major depression.

sublevels.name: Depression
sublevels.description: Depression refers to a state of low mood that can be accompanied with loss of interest in activities that the individual normally perceived as pleasurable, altered appetite and sleep/wake balance. Its severe form, major depression is classified as a mood disorder.

sublevels.name: Long-term Depression
sublevels.description: Long-term depression (LTD) is the biological process by which certain types of synaptic stimulation – such as prolonged low frequency input – result in a long-lasting decrease in the strength of synaptic transmission. It is thought that the mechanisms underlying LTD, together with those underlying long-term potentiation, may contribute to synaptic plasticity during learning.

sublevels.name: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
sublevels.description: Obsessive compulsive disorder is a psychiatric disease that is characterized by anxiety, fear and repetitive behaviour. Possible symptoms are excessive cleaning, repeated checking or hoarding.

sublevels.name: Schizophrenia
sublevels.description: Schizophrenia is a severe and debilitating psychiatric disorder that involves psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions, accompanied with regressive behaviour.

sublevels.name: Anxiety
sublevels.description: Anxiety is characterized by excessive uneasiness, apprehension or dread. It can be generalized or be directed towards specific, usually imagined or exaggerated threat.

sublevels.name: Military Psychology
sublevels.description: Military psychology is the application of several branches within psychology to understanding and treating the unique stressors that come with conducting military operations

sublevels.name: Rehabilitation Psychology
sublevels.description: Rehabilitation is the process of restoring normal function and improving quality of life for individuals following a disease or an injury. Rehabilitation is commonly used to treat people after a sports injury, spinal cord injury, stroke, or orthopaedic surgery.

sublevels.name: Mental Health
sublevels.description: mental health can be understood as the psychological state of someone who is functioning at a satisfactory level of emotional and behavioural adjustment

sublevels.name: Trauma Psychology
sublevels.description: Trauma is a physiological wound, which can be penetrating or nonpenetrating, caused directly or indirectly by external physical force.

sublevels.name: Work and Organizational Psychology
sublevels.description: Work and Organizational or Industrial Organizational Business Psychology or I/O psychology is the science of human behaviour relating to work and applies psychological theories and principles to organizations and individuals in their places of work as well as the individual's work-life more generally.

sublevels.name: Personality
sublevels.description: Personality refers to individual differences in characteristic patterns of thinking, feeling and behaving. It can also refer to how the patterns in different domains combine in each individual.

sublevels.name: Intelligence
sublevels.description: Intelligence is the the mental capacity for abstract reasoning, planning ability, logical thought, conceptual complexity and problem solving. High intelligence is thought to be associated with flexible, adaptive and goal-directed behaviour, particularly in new situations.

sublevels.name: Forgetting
sublevels.description: Forgetting refers to the loss of, or inability to access, information stored in memory. This may occur through a passive process by which the original memory trace is degraded, or by an active process by which new memories interfere with the retrieval of old ones.

sublevels.name: Habituation
sublevels.description: Habituation occurs upon repeated presentation of stimulus such that the innate physiological or behavioural response to that stimulus is gradually diminished.

sublevels.name: Dyslexia
sublevels.description: Dyslexia is a disorder characterized by an impaired ability to comprehend written and printed words or phrases despite intact vision. It can be developmental or acquired, but in either case it interferes with academic achievement or with activities of daily living that require reading skills.

sublevels.name: Fear Conditioning
sublevels.description: Fear conditioning is a type of classical conditioning that involves pairing an aversive stimulus (such as an electric shock) with either a neutral context (such as a location) or stimulus (such as a tone). This results in the expression of a fear response in the presence of the context or stimulus alone.

sublevels.name: Motivation
sublevels.description: Motivation is the driving force that elicits a certain behaviour from an organism in order to satisfy the drive or seek a particular goal. Motivation can be induced by physiological drives such as hunger, thirst or pain, as well as by events in the external environment.

sublevels.name: Decision Making
sublevels.description: Decision making is the process of choosing among alternatives associated with different outcomes. Deciding among multiple options can take the form of selecting a course of action or judging among ideas.

sublevels.name: Habituation
sublevels.description: Habituation occurs upon repeated presentation of stimulus such that the innate physiological or behavioural response to that stimulus is gradually diminished.

sublevels.name: Sport Psychology
sublevels.description: Sport Psychologyis is concerned with the preconditions and determining factors of the behaviour and experience of individuals (persons) in sport.  It aims at the adequate unterstanding of the behaviour and the experience of individuals in sport by describing and measuring consistency and variability, by offering explanations, as well as by determining their preconditions and possibilities to predict and shape its future course.  More specifically, Sport Psychology explores the processes of perception and decision making during sports games, the emergence or reduction of emotions (such as fear), the determining factors of an active lifestyle, the impact of sport on the development of children or the personality and group features of successful athletes and teams.

sublevels.name: Mental Training
sublevels.description: The term Mental Training is used to describe a variety of psychological methods, which aim at facilitating and improving performance, resilience, self-awareness, confidence or well-being by optimising social and communicative skills, cognitive skills or motivational and emotional processes.   In Sport Psychology, the narrow definition of Mental Training specifies it as training procedures for optimising the regulation of movement by conciously and repeatedly envisioning movement tasks or actions. Mental Training may also include techniques to regulate emotion (anger, fear, stress), motivation (will, achievement motivation) or perception (focus, concentration) and strengthen the athletes confidence in his or her capability. This may also include techniques that focus on coach-athlete or team interaction. Besides the long term systematic application of mental training, it is also used situationally in competition preparation or evaluation.

sublevels.name: Perception
sublevels.description: Perception is the process by which the nature and meaning of sensory stimuli are recognized and interpreted. Perception can be influenced by attention and can occur subliminally, without conscious awareness.

sublevels.name: Psychophysics
sublevels.description: Psychophysics is a field of methodology within psychology concerned with studying the sensation of stimuli. Psychophysics methods typically record the effect of systematic modulation of stimuli on a subject’s perception.

sublevels.name: Attention
sublevels.description: Attention is a cognitive process in which a person or animal concentrates on one thing in particular. To attend to something is to focus, heed or take notice of that thing irrespective of what else is going on in the surroundings.

sublevels.name: Motivation
sublevels.description: Motivation is the driving force that elicits a certain behaviour from an organism in order to satisfy the drive or seek a particular goal. Motivation can be induced by physiological drives such as hunger, thirst or pain, as well as by events in the external environment.

sublevels.name: Long-term Memory
sublevels.description: Long-term memory is information encoded in the brain on the time-scale of years. It consists of explicit (declarative) memories that are consciously reportable and depend heavily on the medial temporal lobe and hippocampus and implicit (procedural) memories that are unconscious and depend on the basal ganglia and cerebellum.

sublevels.name: Working Memory
sublevels.description: Working memory is the active and robust retention of multiple bits of information over the time-scale of a few seconds. It is distinguished from short-term memory by the involvement of executive or attentional control that makes the information flexible yet resistant to interference.

sublevels.name: Emotion
sublevels.description: An emotion is an affective state triggered by perceived or recalled external stimuli. Emotions can serve to arouse or motivate behaviours. Examples include sadness, joy, fear, anger and disgust.

sublevels.name: Social Learning
sublevels.description: Social Learning means learning and skill acquisition by imitating and reproducing the peers' behaviors.

sublevels.name: Classical Conditioning
sublevels.description: Classical conditioning is a form of associative learning in which a neutral stimulus (conditioned stimulus, CS) is paired with another stimulus (unconditioned stimulus, US) that brings about an automatic, unlearned response. After the association is learned, the CS is sufficient to elicit the automatic response that is normally elicited by the US.

sublevels.name: Intelligence
sublevels.description: Intelligence is the the mental capacity for abstract reasoning, planning ability, logical thought, conceptual complexity and problem solving. High intelligence is thought to be associated with flexible, adaptive and goal-directed behaviour, particularly in new situations.

sublevels.name: Behavioral Genetics
sublevels.description: Behavioural genetics is the interdisciplinary effort to establish causal links between genes and animal (including human) behavioural traits and neural mechanisms. Methods used include twin studies, quantitative trait mapping by linkage to allelic variants, transgenic animals and targeted gene disruption or silencing.

sublevels.name: Psychological Methods
sublevels.description: Behavioural methods are methods used to study the neural, molecular, genetic or physiological mechanisms that underlie behaviour in humans or other animals (the field of behavioural neuroscience), or methods used to study the psychology of behaviour.

sublevels.name: Psychophysics
sublevels.description: Psychophysics is a field of methodology within psychology concerned with studying the sensation of stimuli. Psychophysics methods typically record the effect of systematic modulation of stimuli on a subject’s perception.

sublevels.name: Health Psychology
sublevels.description: Health psychology is the study of psychological and behavioral processes in health, illness, and healthcare. It is concerned with understanding how psychological, behavioral, and cultural factors contribute to physical health and illness

Gothic Studies

Environmental Communication
sublevels.description: Environmental communication refers to the study and practice of communication about the environment and human interactions with the environment.

sublevels.name: Sports Communication
sublevels.description: Sports communication is an area of study that seeks to understand the relationship between communication processes and sport contexts. Communication processes refer to the creation and understanding of meaning through exchanging verbal and nonverbal messages. It can encompass the study of interpersonal and organizational communication between players, coaches, managers, referees, trainers and physiotherapists, and governing bodies, as well as communication between sports participants, fans, and the media and way in which sports are represented and communicated in the media. the methods used to study Sports Communication range from quantitative over qualitative approaches up to frameworks in critical and cultural studies. Studies in sports communication have addressed subjects such as audience reactions to mediated sporting contests; communication between coaches and athletes; media portrayals of athletes based on considerations such as gender, race, and nationality; and the professional routines of sports media practitioners.

sublevels.name: Political Communication
sublevels.description: Political communication is concerned with how information spreads and influences politics and policy makers, the news media and citizens.

sublevels.name: Development Communication
sublevels.description: Development Communication refers to the use of communication to facilitate social development. Development communication techniques include information dissemination and education, behaviour change, social marketing, social mobilization, media advocacy, communication for social change and community participation.

sublevels.name: Energy Justice
sublevels.description: Energy justice applies justice principles to energy policy and security, its production and systems, energy consumption through the society, and energy activism, and is strongly related to sustainable living and mitigation of climate change.

sublevels.name: Computer Ethics

sublevels.name: Sports Ethics
sublevels.description: Sports Ethics deals with any type of ethical issue, questions or problem in the context of Sport and attempts to suggest sensible courses of actions in order to alleviate or regulate these problems and establish ethical standards. Ethical issues in Sports commonly concern performance enhancing drugs (doping), Gender Discrimination, Fair Play, Responsibility for the performance, Fan Behaviour, Diversity or Protection of athletes health and safety.

sublevels.name: Game Theory
sublevels.description: Game theory is the study of mathematical models of strategic interaction between rational decision-makers. It has applications in all fields of social science, as well as in logic and computer science. Originally, it addressed zero-sum games, in which one person's gains result in losses for the other participants. Today, game theory applies to a wide range of behavioral relations, and is now an umbrella term for the science of logical decision making in humans, animals, and computers

sublevels.name: Literary Diction
sublevels.description: Diction is a writer's or speaker's distinctive vocabulary choices and style of expression in a literary work, poem or story. In its common meaning, it is the distinctiveness of speech.

sublevels.name: Digital Humanities

sublevels.name: Political Science

sublevels.description: Sustainability is essentially the ability to endure, for example by exploiting resources in a way that does not deplete their future availability or unduly damage the wider environment. This concept has been incorporated in the idea of sustainable development.

sublevels.name: Time Series Analysis
sublevels.description: A time series is a sequence of measurements performed at successive points in time. Time series can be used to derive models to predict future values based on previously observed values. Time series are used in statistics, signal processing, pattern recognition, econometrics, mathematical finance, weather forecasting, earthquake prediction, electroencephalography, control engineering, astronomy, communications engineering, and largely in any domain of applied science and engineering which involves temporal measurements

sublevels.name: Game Theory
sublevels.description: Game theory is the study of mathematical models of strategic interaction between rational decision-makers. It has applications in all fields of social science, as well as in logic and computer science. Originally, it addressed zero-sum games, in which one person's gains result in losses for the other participants. Today, game theory applies to a wide range of behavioral relations, and is now an umbrella term for the science of logical decision making in humans, animals, and computers

sublevels.description: Intellectual property (IP), such as patents, provides legal rights to the exclusive use of the output of creative efforts. For example, a patent on a drug could provide its owner with the right to exclusively market that drug for a defined period of time in exchange for detailed public disclosure of the drug’s characteristics, such as chemical structure.
